questions.q: What permissions does a brand-new IAM user have by default?
options: Zero permissions — it can't do anything until access is explicitly granted
Full administrator access, same as root
Read-only access to all S3 buckets
Access to billing data only
questions.explain: Unlike root, a new IAM user starts locked down; access must be explicitly granted through attached policies.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of using an IAM group instead of attaching policies to each user individually?
options: Attach a policy once to the group, and every user in it inherits that access, avoiding drift between individually-managed copies
Groups allow unlimited root access for all members
Groups remove the need for any IAM policies entirely
Groups are only usable with AWS CLI, not the console
questions.explain: Groups centralize permission management: update the group's policy once instead of updating every member's permissions separately.

questions.q: In an IAM policy statement, what does the Resource field specify?
options: Which specific AWS resource(s) the statement applies to, typically written as an ARN
The name of the IAM user the policy belongs to
The dollar amount allowed to be spent
The AWS region where the policy was created
questions.explain: Resource narrows a statement to specific resources, such as a particular S3 bucket, using an Amazon Resource Name (ARN).

questions.q: In this policy snippet — Effect: Allow, Action: s3:GetObject, Resource: arn:aws:s3:::ltv-reports-bucket/* — what can a user with this policy do?
options: Read (download) objects from the ltv-reports-bucket bucket only, and nothing else
Delete any object in any S3 bucket
Create new S3 buckets anywhere in the account
Access every AWS service in the account
questions.explain: The statement allows only s3:GetObject, scoped only to the ltv-reports-bucket resource — a narrow, least-privilege grant.

questions.q: If one policy says Allow for an action and another policy attached to the same identity says Deny for that same action, which wins?
options: Deny always wins, regardless of which policy it came from
Allow always wins because it was likely added first
The result is random each time the action runs
Whichever policy was attached most recently wins
questions.explain: In AWS IAM evaluation logic, an explicit Deny overrides any Allow, no matter where either statement is defined.
